title: What If You Flew a Plane Straight Into a Hurricane's Eye?

scenes.text: What if you flew a plane straight into a hurricane's eye? The scariest part isn't the eye.
Scientists do it for real. NOAA's P-3 turboprops fly in at 8,000 to 10,000 feet, in winds that can top 150 miles an hour.
The worst is the wall of cloud around the eye. One crew compared that ride to a fast wooden roller coaster.
Then it suddenly eases. Inside, the air feels calm, with patches of blue sky and ocean below you.
The eye is only about 5 to 30 miles wide, ringed by the storm's fiercest winds.
Crews fly eight to ten hour missions, twice a day, up to six days in a row. The calm was only the middle of the storm.
